items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: External key management for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM
items.headline: External key management for Key Vault Managed HSM is generally available
items.summary: External key management for Azure Key Vault Managed HSM is now generally available in all Azure public regions. It targets organizations with regulatory or sovereignty requirements to keep physical control of their key-encryption keys. The item text is truncated, so the list of supported Azure services and any operational limits need checking at the source.
items.architecture_impact: Where key custody must stay with the organization, key-encryption keys can remain outside Azure rather than inside the HSM, which changes the key trust boundary and the operating model for key lifecycle. Architects should confirm which services support it and the availability and latency implications before committing to it.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: Standard service endpoint
items.headline: Standard service endpoint is generally available for private IaaS-to-PaaS connectivity
items.summary: Standard service endpoint, part of the Azure Private Link family, is now generally available. It is positioned as a scalable and secure way to connect Azure IaaS workloads to Azure PaaS services, addressing manageability and scale limitations.
items.architecture_impact: Architects can now consider this option when designing private connectivity from IaaS workloads to PaaS services, weighing it against existing Private Link and service endpoint choices. Scale limits, pricing and regional availability are not stated in the item and need checking at the source before committing a design.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: Azure Site Recovery Support for Azure ARC-enabled Windows VMWare/Physical servers
items.headline: Azure Site Recovery now protects Arc-enabled Windows VMware VMs and physical servers
items.summary: Azure Site Recovery now supports disaster recovery for Azure Arc-enabled Windows VMware virtual machines and on-premises physical servers. Customers can keep using Azure Arc for governance and inventory while protecting these machines with ASR.
items.architecture_impact: Hybrid designs can use one DR service for Arc-managed Windows VMs and physical servers instead of a separate tool, which changes the DR topology for those workloads. Check the source for supported OS versions, replication targets and any limits, which the item text does not state.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: Managed StandardV2 NAT Gateway for AKS
items.headline: AKS provisions StandardV2 NAT Gateway by default for managed outbound
items.summary: AKS now provisions and manages a StandardV2 NAT Gateway for clusters using an AKS-managed virtual network with the managedNATGateway outbound type. StandardV2 is the default managed NAT Gateway SKU for new clusters in supported regions.
items.architecture_impact: New AKS clusters get StandardV2 NAT Gateway for outbound connectivity by default, so egress design, IP planning and SNAT assumptions should be revisited for new deployments. Existing clusters and the regions supported are not detailed in the text and need checking at the source.

items.title: Retirement: Microsoft Dev Box will be retired on September 18, 2028
items.headline: Microsoft Dev Box retires September 18, 2028; closing down starts September 2026
items.summary: Microsoft Dev Box will retire on September 18, 2028, and the closing-down process begins September 14, 2026. After retirement the service will no longer be available, and it is currently in maintenance mode.
items.architecture_impact: Teams relying on Dev Box for developer workstations need to plan a replacement well before the retirement date. The replacement option is not named in the item text, so check the source for the recommended alternative and migration guidance.

items.title: Retirement: Azure Deployment Environments will be retired on February 22, 2027
items.headline: Azure Deployment Environments retires February 22, 2027; closing down started
items.summary: Azure Deployment Environments will retire on February 22, 2027, and its closing-down process begins September 14, 2026. After retirement the service will no longer be available.
items.architecture_impact: Self-service environment provisioning pipelines built on Azure Deployment Environments will need an alternative provisioning approach before February 2027. The replacement is not named in the item text, so check the source for migration guidance.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines in Azure Bleu
categories: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
items.headline: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines now available in Azure Bleu (France)
items.summary: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines is now generally available in Azure Bleu, France's sovereign cloud environment. It lets customers deploy and manage SQL Server workloads while meeting data residency and sovereignty requirements.
items.architecture_impact: Workloads with French sovereignty or residency requirements gain a SQL Server IaaS option within Azure Bleu rather than a public region. Confirm which other services are available in Azure Bleu and any operational constraints, since the item text does not state them.

items.title: Build and govern AI agents across a multitenant organization
items.headline: Governing AI agents across a multitenant organization with a federated agent factory
items.summary: This reference architecture centralizes agent governance standards and oversight while keeping agent identities, business data and runtime enforcement in each owning tenant. It targets enterprises with subsidiaries that need common controls without merging tenant boundaries.
items.architecture_impact: Use one multitenant identity blueprint that creates tenant-local agent identities, expose narrow governed tools rather than broad credentials, and enforce policy at runtime rather than only at design review. Some capabilities are in preview, so confirm their terms and regional availability before depending on them.

items.title: Retirement: Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 Azure VMs
items.headline: Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3 and Esv3 VM series retire on November 15, 2029
items.summary: Microsoft is retiring the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3 and Esv3 Azure VM series in public cloud regions, which then enter End-of-Life. Workloads on these general-purpose and memory-optimized series need to move to supported successors before the date.
items.architecture_impact: Include these series in migration plans and choose successor sizes in new designs rather than these series. Check the source for the recommended replacement series and any transition guidance, as the text does not name them.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server supports cross-tenant customer-managed keys (CMK)
items.headline: PostgreSQL Flexible Server supports cross-tenant customer-managed keys
items.summary: Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server can now encrypt data with keys held in Azure Key Vault or Azure Managed HSM in a different Microsoft Entra tenant. This lets key custody sit with a separate tenant or organization from the database.
items.architecture_impact: Key ownership can be separated from the database tenant, which helps with split-custody and regulatory designs but adds cross-tenant trust and key-access dependencies to plan. Check the source for supported regions, configuration steps and any limitations, as they are not stated in the text.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: SQL Server on Azure Local Disconnected (ALDO)
items.headline: SQL Server on Azure Local disconnected (ALDO) reaches general availability
items.summary: ALDO extends SQL Server support to environments that cannot maintain continuous connectivity to Azure. It targets highly regulated, secure, remote or air-gapped sites where internet access is restricted.
items.architecture_impact: Disconnected sites can now run supported SQL Server without a constant Azure link, which changes management, licensing and patching assumptions for those sites. Check the source for the operational limits and licensing terms that apply offline.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: SQL Server support on Azure Local connected mode
items.headline: SQL Server on Azure Local connected mode reaches general availability
items.summary: SQL Server workloads can run on Azure Local while using Azure services for management, governance, monitoring, security and licensing. Connectivity to Azure is established through Azure Arc.
items.architecture_impact: Hybrid SQL estates on Azure Local can be governed centrally through Azure Arc, which affects operating model and licensing decisions for on-premises SQL. Confirm the connectivity requirements and supported configurations at the source.

items.title: Retirement: Azure Arc enabled System Center Virtual Machine Manager will be retired September 30, 2029
items.headline: Azure Arc-enabled SCVMM retires on September 30, 2029
items.summary: Microsoft is retiring Azure Arc-enabled System Center Virtual Machine Manager in September 2029. Customers using it for Azure services and management must transition to alternative solutions.
items.architecture_impact: Hybrid designs that rely on Arc-enabled SCVMM for management need a replacement plan well before 2029. The item text is truncated, so the recommended alternatives and migration path need checking at the source.

items.title: Retirement: Azure IoT Central will be retired on September 20, 2029
items.headline: Azure IoT Central retires on September 20, 2029
items.summary: Azure IoT Central will be retired on September 20, 2029, and can be used until that date. Microsoft is shifting future investment toward other Azure IoT offerings.
items.architecture_impact: Solutions built on IoT Central need a transition plan for device onboarding, device management and data flows before the retirement date. The replacement services are not named in the truncated text, so confirm the migration path at the source.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: Support for large volume breakthrough mode
items.headline: Large volume breakthrough mode reaches general availability in Azure NetApp Files
items.summary: Breakthrough mode supports Azure NetApp Files large volumes up to 2 PiB with throughput up to 80 GiBps, depending on workload characteristics. It is aimed at demanding HPC and EDA workloads.
items.architecture_impact: Architects can consider consolidating very large datasets onto single volumes instead of sharding across many, provided the workload fits the throughput profile. Validate the achievable performance against the actual workload, as the figures depend on workload characteristics.

items.title: SQL Server on Azure Local is now generally available
items.headline: SQL Server on Azure Local is generally available
items.summary: SQL Server on Azure Local is now generally available. It lets customers modernize data workloads while keeping control of infrastructure, connectivity and where data is placed.
items.architecture_impact: Data-residency or latency-constrained workloads can stay on-premises under Azure management, which changes the hybrid placement decision for SQL estates. Check supported configurations, licensing and connectivity requirements at the source before committing a design.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: Vector search and vector indexes in Azure SQL
items.headline: Vector search and vector indexes generally available in Azure SQL Database
items.summary: Azure SQL Database now offers generally available vector indexes and approximate nearest neighbour search using T-SQL. This supports AI scenarios such as semantic search directly in the database.
items.architecture_impact: Teams can keep embedding search in the operational database rather than adding a separate vector store, which simplifies data architecture and reduces data movement. Check the source for index limits and performance characteristics before committing.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: Luxembourg - Azure Extended Zones
items.headline: Luxembourg Azure Extended Zone is now generally available
items.summary: The Luxembourg Azure Extended Zone has reached general availability. Extended Zones are small-footprint extensions of Azure placed in metro areas, industry centers or specific jurisdictions for low-latency and data-residency workloads.
items.architecture_impact: Architects with Luxembourg residency or low-latency needs can now consider placing workloads in an Extended Zone rather than a full region. Check at the source which services are available there and what the capacity and resilience limits are before committing.

items.title: From Camera to Canvas: How Multimodal GenAI Automates Shop Floor Instructions
items.headline: Multimodal GenAI pipeline that turns assembly videos into illustrated work instructions
items.summary: This architecture converts shop-floor assembly videos into timestamped transcripts, structured procedures and illustrated Word and PDF documents. Human approval gates at transcript and procedure stages control quality before documents are produced.
items.architecture_impact: The design uses queue-driven asynchronous processing with retries and human approval as a hard gate, and it recommends automated evaluations for groundedness and safety coverage. Trade-offs include model cost and review effort, and the pattern is reusable for other video-to-document workflows.

items.title: Retirement: Azure Communication Services (ACS) standalone services will be retired on September 30, 2028
items.headline: Standalone Azure Communication Services offerings retire September 30, 2028
items.summary: Microsoft will retire several standalone Azure Communication Services offerings on September 30, 2028, after which they will no longer be available. The item text is truncated, so the full list of affected services needs checking at the source.
items.architecture_impact: Any design that depends on the affected standalone ACS services will need to move to a successor offering before the retirement date. Confirm the replacement path and plan the migration against the 2028 deadline.

items.title: Your architecture diagram is not your resilience
items.headline: Resilience must be maintained over time, not set up once
items.summary: This Azure Well-Architected guidance argues that resilience is a continuously maintained property rather than a one-time setup project. It frames the architecture diagram as only a starting point for reliability.
items.architecture_impact: Teams should plan for ongoing resilience validation, such as reviewing failure modes as systems change, rather than treating the original design as sufficient. The excerpt is truncated, so the specific practices should be checked at the source.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: Publishing Microsoft Foundry agents to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams
items.headline: Foundry agents can now be published to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams
items.summary: Publishing Microsoft Foundry agents to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams is now generally available. Developers can make agents available to end users in these channels without a custom integration path.
items.architecture_impact: Agent solutions can now be delivered directly into Microsoft 365 surfaces, which affects channel and identity design for those agents. Check at the source how access control and governance apply to published agents before standardising on this route.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: High-scale mesh in Azure Virtual Network Manager
items.headline: High-scale mesh connectivity in Azure Virtual Network Manager is generally available
items.summary: High-scale mesh using connected groups is now generally available in Azure Virtual Network Manager. In available regions, customers can connect up to 3,000 virtual networks in a single mesh connectivity configuration by default, with higher-scale IP connectivity also mentioned.
items.architecture_impact: Large multi-network estates can use one mesh configuration instead of many hub-and-spoke or peering layers, which changes the trade-off between topology simplicity and routing control. Confirm regional availability and the exact higher-scale limits at the source before relying on them.

items.title: Microsoft Foundry Observability: How to Trace, Evaluate, Monitor, and Secure AI Agents
items.headline: Five-layer observability model for tracing, evaluating and monitoring AI agents in Foundry
items.summary: The article argues that agents can be technically healthy yet semantically wrong, so observability must cover agent execution, safety, quality and business outcome as well as availability. It pairs Microsoft Foundry traces and evaluations with Application Insights, Log Analytics and Azure Monitor alerts, using OpenTelemetry as the common trace model.
items.architecture_impact: Architects should add agent-level tracing of tool calls and arguments, policy checks and evaluation signals alongside APM, rather than relying on HTTP status and latency. Exact limits, pricing and feature availability are not stated in the text and need checking at the source.

items.title: Building on AI Landing Zones: Operationalizing Enterprise AI with the Citadel Architecture
items.headline: Citadel reference architecture for a shared enterprise AI operating model on Azure
items.summary: Citadel is an opinionated reference architecture that composes Microsoft Foundry and complementary Azure services with AI landing zones into a shared enterprise AI operating model. It addresses where shared access controls sit, how usage is attributed, who owns agent identity, and how platform owners and application teams divide responsibilities.
items.architecture_impact: Architects can adopt selected Citadel patterns, such as a shared AI gateway and cross-team observability, on top of an existing landing zone without replacing it. The key decision is which additional patterns the operating model needs, and confirming which requests actually pass through the gateway.

items.title: [Launched] Generally Available: TLS/SSL certificate and end-to-end TLS encryption support for Azure Functions Flex Consumption
items.headline: Azure Functions Flex Consumption gains GA TLS/SSL certificates and end-to-end TLS
items.summary: Azure Functions Flex Consumption now supports TLS/SSL certificates through a new site-scoped certificate model, with end-to-end TLS encryption, generally available. Each function app can hold up to 3 private (.pfx) and 3 public (.cer) certificates, uploaded directly or imported from other sources (details truncated; check the source).
items.architecture_impact: Workloads that needed custom certificates or end-to-end TLS, for example client certificates or encrypted backend hops, can now run on Flex Consumption rather than Premium or App Service plans. Check that the per-app certificate limits fit your design.

items.title: Your Private Endpoint Does Not Cover Agent Egress: Locking Down Azure AI Foundry in Both Directions
items.headline: Securing Foundry agent egress with network injection, beyond private endpoints
items.summary: A private endpoint on a Foundry resource secures only inbound client traffic, while agent outbound calls need network injection into a delegated subnet. The article walks through private DNS for the inbound path and a bring-your-own-VNet setup so agents can call an MCP server in another VNet from private addresses.
items.architecture_impact: Architects must decide network injection at creation time, because it cannot be added to an existing Foundry account, and private networking forces the standard setup with bring-your-own dependent resources. Inbound and outbound paths need separate validation, including DNS zones for all Foundry endpoint names.

items.title: Choosing the Right Agent in Microsoft Foundry
items.headline: Choosing between Prompt Agents and Hosted Agents in Microsoft Foundry Agent Service
items.summary: The article frames the choice between declarative Prompt Agents with a managed runtime and code-based Hosted Agents that Foundry runs as an endpoint. It recommends deciding based on where orchestration logic, state and operations ownership should sit, with examples of when each fits.
items.architecture_impact: Use Prompt Agents when behaviour can be expressed through instructions and supported tools, and move to Hosted Agents when branching, deterministic state machines, custom middleware or custom payloads appear. Hosted Agents shift patching, testing and dependency ownership to the engineering team.

items.title: Token Economics in Practice
items.headline: Token economics for agents: controlling cost per accepted task on Azure
items.summary: The article argues that cost per accepted task, not cost per token, is the right unit for agent economics, and proposes a controller that forecasts cost distributions and enforces routing, caching and budget policies against quality floors. It maps the controller to Azure components including API Management, App Configuration, Foundry evaluations and Azure Monitor.
items.architecture_impact: Architects should route agent traffic through a gateway that enforces externalized cost policies and feeds telemetry into evaluation, so savings are reverted when quality drops. The modelled percentile budgets are planning estimates and need calibrating against real traces before being treated as guarantees.

items.title: Preserve a Legacy IP During Azure Migration with Private Link Service Direct Connect
items.headline: Keeping a legacy private IP during migration with Private Link Service Direct Connect
items.summary: The article demonstrates using Private Link Service Direct Connect with a Private Endpoint so migrated web and application tiers keep reaching an on-premises database on its original private address. Traffic reaches the on-premises resource over a site-to-site VPN from a hub VNet, which also handles overlapping address space without peering.
items.architecture_impact: This is a bridge pattern: it allows the application tier to move before its backend, but it adds a hub routing dependency and should be retired once the dependency is modernised. The capability is in public preview with limited regions, so regional availability and requirements need checking at the source before production use.
